NOISE POLLUTION OR RELIGIOUS POLICING? THE DOUBLE STANDARD MUST END. 🔊⚖️

Delhi Police says it intervened at the CR Park Durga Puja pandal because loud music allegedly continued beyond the permitted hours.

Fine. Enforce the law. But enforce it EQUALLY.

Now look at the disturbing questions this raises:

🔸 KANWAR YATRA: In August 2026, Hindustan Times recorded DJ-truck noise peaks of 110 decibels during the Kanwar Yatra in Delhi—far above the stated residential-area limits. Residents complained of sleepless nights. Were the same standards enforced consistently against every procession?

🔸 MOSQUE & AZAAN: In October, a muezzin in Uttar Pradesh was reportedly arrested after officials heard an allegedly loud azaan; the mosque’s loudspeaker was seized. Meanwhile, noise from large religious processions can be framed as celebration and devotion. Why does enforcement so often become a public controversy when the issue involves a mosque?

🔸 WEST BENGAL: In August, police asked mosques in several districts to limit or replace rooftop loudspeakers under noise-pollution rules. If the government is serious about noise, where is the same transparent, measurable, religion-neutral enforcement across ALL religious venues and processions?

🔸 DURGA PUJA: Delhi Police says its action at CR Park was about court-mandated noise limits. Then publish the applicable orders, measured sound levels, timings and enforcement records. Let the public judge whether the rules are being applied fairly.

Let me be absolutely clear: I am not demanding that Hindu festivals be restricted, nor that mosques be exempt from noise rules. I am demanding equal treatment for everyone.

A Kanwar Yatra procession is not above the law.
A Durga Puja pandal is not above the law.
A mosque loudspeaker is not above the law.
And the police are not above public scrutiny.

Religious freedom does not mean an unlimited right to impose loud sound on unwilling residents. The right to peace and quiet does not mean the state can selectively target one community while excusing another.

The real test is simple:

If 110 dB from a DJ procession is a violation, act on it. If a loudspeaker at a pandal exceeds the limit, act on it. If a mosque exceeds the same limit, act on it. Use the same rules, the same evidence and the same consequences.

No selective outrage. No religious privilege. No political interference.

Delhi Police. UP Police. West Bengal Police. Show the public the data: how many complaints, inspections, notices, fines and prosecutions involve each type of religious event?

If enforcement is fair, transparent data will prove it. If it is selective, the public deserves to know.

THE LAW MUST BE BLIND TO RELIGION—not blind to noise when the crowd is politically convenient.

#NoisePollution #EqualTreatment #RuleOfLaw #DelhiPolice #UPPolice #WestBengalPolice #ReligiousFreedom #Hypocrisy
